# Prompt Injection Defenses in Agent Orchestrators

## Executive Summary

Multi-agent orchestrators create attack surfaces that do not exist in
single-agent systems. When agents orchestrate other agents and execute
privileged tools, prompt injection becomes a systems security problem — not
just an NLP problem. This analysis covers seven dimensions of orchestrator
security across 47 sources, including 22 peer-reviewed papers.

**Key finding:** Architectural defenses (privilege separation, capability-based
security, mandatory access control) achieve 0% attack success rate on
benchmarks, while detection-based defenses are routinely bypassed. However, no
architectural defense has confirmed production deployment. The gap between
research effectiveness and production adoption is the central challenge.

### Defense Effectiveness Summary

| Defense Category | Best ASR | Utility Cost | Maturity |
|---|---|---|---|
| MAC/ABAC (SEAgent) [4] | 0% | +10.7% goal success | Research |
| DSL policies (Progent) [7] | 0% | Preserved | Research |
| Capability tokens (CaMeL) [15] | Provable | −7pp (77% vs 84%)* | Research |
| LLM guardrail (PromptArmor) [16] | <1% | Preserved | Research |
| Multi-layer framework [17] | 8.7% | −5.7% (94.3% retained) | Research |
| Tool filter (AgentDojo) [8] | 6.84% | +4pp (73% vs 69%) | Research |
| Prompt Shields (Microsoft) [25] | Unknown | Low | Production (GA) |
| Semantic Kernel Filters [26] | N/A (deterministic) | None | Production |
| Gemini layered defense [19] | Varies* | Low | Production |
| AWS Bedrock Guardrails [35] | Unknown | Low | Production |

\* Google reports TAP achieves ~100% ASR against undefended Gemini 2.0 but
doesn't publish defended ASR numbers [19]. CaMeL utility numbers from
search snippet; not verified against full paper text.

## Methodology

Seven research dimensions were investigated using web sources visited in
session. Discovery agents (Sonnet) identified candidate sources across 56
search queries; analysis agents (Opus) extracted data from fetched pages.
Two independent verification agents audited the output.

Sources span: 22 Tier 1 (peer-reviewed/government), 15 Tier 2 (vendor
documentation), 8 Tier 3 (industry research), 2 Tier 4 (community). Several
OWASP pages and vendor sites were inaccessible during the session.

## 1. Orchestrator-Specific Attack Vectors

Multi-agent orchestrators introduce five attack categories absent in
single-agent systems:

### 1.1 Control-Flow Hijacking

Untrusted inputs (web content, files, emails) can hijack multi-agent
coordination [1]. Magentic-One with GPT-4o executes malicious code from local
files 97% of the time [1]. Round-Robin orchestrator with GPT-4o-mini reaches
100% [1]. Critically, "these attacks succeed even if individual agents are not
susceptible to direct or indirect prompt injection, and even if they refuse to
perform harmful actions" [1].

**Orchestrator capability paradox:** More advanced orchestrators execute
multi-step attack chains more reliably [1]. This inverts the usual assumption
that better models are safer.

### 1.2 Inter-Agent Communication Attacks

Agent-in-the-Middle (AiTM) attacks intercept and manipulate inter-agent
messages using an LLM-powered adversarial agent [2]. Framework-agnostic across
AutoGen and Camel [2]. Chain-structured topologies show highest vulnerability.

### 1.3 Tool Selection Manipulation

ToolHijacker injects malicious tool documents into tool libraries [3]. MCP
tool descriptions contain hidden instructions invisible to users but visible
to AI [28]. Tool shadowing redirects trusted tool behavior — e.g., all emails
sent to attacker-controlled addresses [28].

### 1.4 Memory and Context Poisoning

Three distinct attack patterns exploit agent memory:

| Attack | ASR | Mechanism | Persistence |
|---|---|---|---|
| MINJA [9] | 70% (>95% ISR) | Query-only memory injection | Session |
| AgentPoison [10] | ≥80% | RAG knowledge base backdoor | Persistent |
| ARCJ [11] | +23-53% vs baseline | Self-replicating viral propagation | Cross-agent |

AgentPoison achieves ≥80% ASR with <0.1% poison rate and <1% benign
degradation — no model training required [10].

### 1.5 Approval Bypass

HITL approval gates are bypassable. "Lies-in-the-loop" attacks instruct agents
to mislead users during approval dialogs [41]. Pre-approved commands exploited
for RCE via argument injection (e.g., `go test -exec`) [29]. Trail of Bits
concludes "maintaining safe command allowlists is fundamentally flawed" [29].

### Relationship to Single-Agent Injection

These are not amplified versions of single-agent attacks — they exploit
structural properties unique to orchestrators: inter-agent trust, shared
memory, tool delegation chains, and coordination capabilities. Traditional
indirect prompt injection techniques achieve "near-zero success rate" against
orchestrators compared to orchestrator-specific attacks [1].

## 2. Production Orchestrator Defenses

### What Vendors Have Deployed

**OpenAI:** Instruction hierarchy (System > Developer > User > Tool) trained
into models [33]. Agents SDK with guardrails as first-class concepts,
optimistic execution, fail-fast [46]. Acknowledges prompt injection "unlikely
to ever be fully solved" [34].

**Microsoft:** Prompt Shields (GA March 2024) with Spotlighting [25]. Semantic
Kernel filters provide deterministic code-level enforcement [26]. Published
comprehensive defense-in-depth pattern (March 2026) with 9 specific controls
[25].

**AWS:** Bedrock Guardrails with prompt attack filter at four strength levels
[35]. **Critical gap:** guardrails not applied to tool input/output — only
user input and final answer [35].

**Google:** Layered defense for Gemini with content classifiers (10% FPR),
security thought reinforcement, URL redaction [19]. ADK with OAuth-based
identity, before/after tool callbacks, plugin architecture [27].

### The Deployment Gap

Production defenses focus overwhelmingly on input filtering and user
confirmation. Architectural defenses (privilege separation, capability tokens,
MAC) that achieve 0% ASR in research remain undeployed in production.

Evidence of the gap: 57.3% of organizations have agents in production, while
NIST found all 13 frontier models successfully attacked at least once [47].

## 3. Least-Privilege Tool Access

### Academic Frameworks

Five frameworks published 2025-2026, none with confirmed production deployment:

**SEAgent** [4] — MAC via ABAC with information flow graphs. 0% ASR. 0% FPR
for 1-2 tools, 5.13% for ≥3 tools. Outperforms IsolateGPT (2-4× slower,
18% FPR) while improving multi-agent goal success by 10.7%.

**Progent** [7] — DSL for fine-grained policies. 0% ASR on AgentDojo, ASB,
AgentPoison. LLMs can automatically generate effective policies.

**CaMeL** [15] — Dual-LLM with capability sandbox. Provable security but 7pp
utility cost (77% vs 84%).

**MiniScope** [6] — Automatic permission hierarchy construction. 1-6% latency
overhead.

**PFI** [5] — Privileged/unprivileged access tokens. System security approach.

### Approval Gates

Available in AWS Bedrock (`requireConfirmation`), OpenAI Agents SDK
(`needsApproval`), Claude Code (default on). All opt-in except Claude Code.
HITL is one layer, not a complete solution — lies-in-the-loop demonstrates
agents can mislead during approval [41].

### MCP Security Gaps

MCP lacks native RBAC and fine-grained authorization [36]. Servers request
overly broad scopes. No authenticated delegation protocol. Confused deputy
risk inherent in the server-as-deputy model.

## 4. Prompt Injection Detection

### Classifier Performance

State-of-the-art classifiers show dramatic performance gaps between benchmarks
and real-world conditions:

| Detector | Benchmark Performance | Indirect Injection Rate | Over-Defense |
|---|---|---|---|
| ProtectAI DeBERTa v2 | 99.93% accuracy | — | — |
| PromptGuard 2 (Meta) | Low FPR (0.4%) | 37.3% detection | 0.88% accuracy* |
| LlamaGuard | 3.0% FPR | 27.4% detection | — |
| InjecGuard [20] | 83.48% avg | — | 87.32% accuracy |

\* On NotInject benchmark: 339 benign samples with trigger words. Random
guessing = 50%.

Standard evaluation overestimates performance by 8+ percentage points vs
Leave-One-Dataset-Out evaluation [21].

### LLM-Based Detection

PromptArmor achieves <1% FPR and FNR on AgentDojo using GPT-4o/4.1/o4-mini
[16]. Recommended as standard baseline. However, LLM-based guardrails can
themselves be prompt-injected — a recursive defense problem.

### Multi-Agent Detection Gap

No detection method is specifically designed for orchestrator-to-agent
communication patterns. Self-replicating prompt infections spread through
multi-agent systems like a computer virus [11]. Neither LLM Tagging nor
traditional defenses alone are sufficient.

## 5. Framework Security Boundaries

### Enforced vs. Advisory

Most framework "guardrails" are advisory — the model follows them because the
response is statistically likely, not because enforcement prevents violation.

**Deterministic enforcement:** Semantic Kernel filters [26], SEAgent ABAC [4],
capability tokens [15][43], sandbox kernel boundaries.

**Probabilistic/advisory:** Prompt-based guardrails, system instructions,
role definitions, few-shot examples.

### CVE Evidence

March 2026 saw multiple CVEs across major frameworks:

- **LangChain/LangGraph:** CVE-2026-34070 (path traversal, CVSS 7.5),
  CVE-2025-67644 (SQL injection, CVSS 7.3), CVE-2025-68664 (deserialization,
  CVSS 9.3)
- **CrewAI:** CVE-2026-2275 (arbitrary C function calls when Docker
  unreachable), three additional sandbox escape CVEs

Child agents inherit parent's full credentials with no scope narrowing in
CrewAI. AutoGen Studio is explicitly "not meant for production."

### OWASP Agentic Top 10 (December 2025)

Ten agentic-specific risks: ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse,
ASI03 Identity/Privilege Abuse, ASI04 Supply Chain, ASI05 Unexpected Code
Execution, ASI06 Memory/Context Poisoning, ASI07-09 Data security, ASI10
Rogue Agents [37].

## 6. Confused Deputy Problem

LLMs are "inherently confusable deputies" — the UK NCSC concludes this may
never be fully fixed because LLMs have no separation between data and
instructions [23].

### Orchestrator-Specific Amplification

- **Delegation chain compounding:** Risk at every hop (A → B → C) [44]
- **Cross-agent privilege escalation:** Compromised agent reconfigures others [44]
- **Session smuggling:** Sub-agents embed malicious actions in routine responses [44]
- **Capability amplification:** Better orchestrators = more reliable attacks [1]

### Mitigations

**Capability-based security** (CaMeL [15], Tenuo [43]) binds authority to
unforgeable tokens. The LLM can be fooled at the language layer, but cannot
forge capabilities [43].

**Privilege drop:** When processing untrusted data, privileges drop to that
party's level [23].

**MAC enforcement:** SEAgent blocks specific flow patterns (untrusted →
trusted → sensitive tool) with 0% ASR [4].

## 7. Defense-in-Depth Architecture

### Recommended Stack

Based on evidence across all dimensions, for an orchestrator executing real
actions (shell scripts, API calls, AAP jobs):

| Priority | Control | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Architectural separation (dual-LLM or agent isolation) | CaMeL provable [15], PFI [5] |
| 2 | Deterministic tool controls (ABAC/DSL, not prompts) | SEAgent 0% ASR [4], Progent 0% [7] |
| 3 | Tool output sanitization | Near-complete mitigation [17] |
| 4 | Sandbox code execution (microVM or gVisor) | Multiple vendors converging |
| 5 | Short-lived credentials scoped to task | CSA ATF [30], NCSC [23] |
| 6 | Detection layer (LLM guardrail + canary tokens) | PromptArmor <1% FPR [16] |
| 7 | HITL for irreversible actions (one layer, not sole defense) | Bypassable [41] |
| 8 | Monitoring and behavioral baselines | Microsoft [25], CSA [30] |

Key design principle: "Design with the expectation that prompt injection
attacks are inevitable" [25].

### Progressive Breach Containment

Address each breach stage [40]:
1. **Compromised intent** → Input filtering + architectural separation
2. **Tool access** → Deterministic access control + sandbox
3. **Cross-agent propagation** → Agent isolation + monitoring
4. **Cascading failures** → Circuit breakers + short-lived credentials

## Relationship to Existing Research

The existing [prompt-injection-defenses](../prompt-injection-defenses/)
research covers general defenses for LLM agents fetching external content.
This analysis extends that work into orchestrator-specific territory:

| Aspect | General Defenses | Orchestrator-Specific |
|---|---|---|
| Attack surface | User input, external content | + Inter-agent messages, tool chains, shared memory |
| Confused deputy | Single agent misuse | + Delegation chains, session smuggling |
| Privilege model | Agent has tools | + Multi-agent credential delegation |
| Propagation | Single session | + Viral cross-agent, persistent memory |
| Detection | Input classifiers | + Inter-agent message inspection |

The general defense comparison table (CaMeL 0% ASR, Spotlighting 3-8%,
Instruction Hierarchy +63% improvement, classifiers bypassed 70-88%) remains
valid. This analysis adds orchestrator-specific attack vectors and the
framework security boundary analysis.

## Open Problems

1. **No production architectural defense.** Every 0% ASR defense is research-only.
   The hardest problem is not building the defense but deploying it without
   breaking existing agent functionality.

2. **Detection in orchestrator contexts.** Classifiers designed for user-to-agent
   injection fail on inter-agent and tool-output injection surfaces [21].

3. **Credential delegation protocol.** No standard exists for scoped, revocable
   credential delegation in multi-agent chains.

4. **Runtime intent verification.** Determining whether an authorized action
   aligns with the user's actual goal is an open research problem — traditional
   access control only checks permission, not intent.

5. **Adaptive attack arms race.** Defenses effective on static benchmarks
   routinely fail under adaptive attacks [19]. The NIST Gray Swan competition
   showed all 13 frontier models can be attacked [47].

6. **Regulatory pressure without standards.** EU AI Act enforcement begins
   August 2, 2026. OWASP Agentic Top 10 published December 2025. Framework
   compliance tools remain immature.
